analysis.one_liner: Locks in existing federal fuel economy and vehicle emissions standards through model year 2025.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 64 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and no Republicans, sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2012, federal agencies set rules requiring new cars and light trucks to average about 46 miles per gallon by 2025 and to emit less carbon. In 2018, the administration was moving to weaken those rules. This bill would write the existing standards into law and bar federal agencies from taking any action that reduces how strict they are.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who save money on gasoline over the life of their cars; communities affected by air pollution; and anyone exposed to climate change, since the standards were projected to cut greenhouse gases by 540 million metric tons and oil use by 1.2 billion barrels over the lifetime of the vehicles covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and communities breathing vehicle exhaust

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require fuel economy standards for model years 2021 through 2025 at least as strong as the 2012 rules, with a fleet-wide average target of 46.3 miles per gallon by 2025.
It would bar NHTSA and EPA from taking any action that could effectively reduce the stringency of the standards, including by loosening credit rules that let automakers dilute compliance.
The 2012 standards were projected to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 540 million metric tons and oil consumption by 1.2 billion barrels over the vehicles' lifetimes.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to keep meeting the standards rather than building and selling less efficient vehicles, and the oil industry, which would sell 1.2 billion fewer barrels of fuel. Some of the compliance cost can show up in new-car prices.

drawbacks.text: Meeting stricter fuel economy rules raises manufacturing costs, and some of that cost can be passed to buyers through higher new-car prices — a real cost, though the standards' projected fuel savings were intended to outweigh it over the life of the vehicle.

The bill would not simply set policy going forward; it would lock in the text of 2012 rules and forbid agencies from revising them for any reason through 2025, removing the flexibility regulators normally have to adjust standards if the underlying assumptions prove wrong.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — lower gasoline spending for drivers and lower emissions — is large and well-documented in the bill's own findings, and the 2012 standards were adopted after negotiation with automakers themselves. The costs fall on automakers and oil producers, with some pass-through to new-car prices. The main design weakness is rigidity: hard-coding the standards into statute leaves no room for regulatory adjustment, but the bill was written precisely because the agencies were preparing to weaken the standards.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and passed to a subcommittee the next day — then nothing happened for the remaining ten months of the Congress, so it died without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on March 8, 2018, with 19 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and to the Subcommittee on Environment on March 9, 2018.
63 additional House members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
No further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and oil companies benefit from the bill's failure, because the fuel economy and emissions standards it would have locked in were later weakened instead. Car buyers lose the fuel savings the standards would have delivered.

for.name: Rep. Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write the existing vehicle fuel economy and emissions standards into law.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never took it up; it died there for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 64 supporters — the sponsor and 63 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would keep automakers bound to the fuel economy and emissions standards they had agreed to in 2012 but were seeking relief from; weaker standards let them sell less efficient vehicles. Some compliance costs can reach buyers through new-car prices.

The standards were projected to cut oil consumption by 1.2 billion barrels over the vehicles' lifetimes, meaning less gasoline sold. The industry's gain from weaker standards comes at the expense of drivers' fuel bills.
